messages.content:
You are evaluating a PTSD case vignette for the presence of causal
connections between five Ehlers & Clark cognitive components: Triggers, Negative Appraisals, Memory,
Threat, and Maladaptive Strategies.

For each of the 20 ordered, directed (A -> B) pairs of distinct components, decide whether the
vignette conveys, in some paragraph, that A influences, drives, or leads to B. Apply the same
causal standard as a structural validator:

COMPONENT SYNONYMS (any of these synonyms count as the component appearing):
  Triggers              -> "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals   -> "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory                -> "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat                -> "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies-> "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "safety behaviours", "maladaptive coping"

CAUSAL STANDARD
An edge A -> B is PRESENT (return 1) iff, within the same paragraph:
  (i) both A and B (or their synonyms) appear; AND
  (ii) the paragraph conveys that A influences / drives / leads to B, through direct causal
       language, sequential structure, or connecting phrases like "because of", "this meant",
       "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
If no paragraph conveys the A -> B relationship, return 0 for that edge.

You will return a binary judgement for each of the 20 ordered pairs. Be strict: do not assume
an edge based on mere co-occurrence; the paragraph must actually convey directional influence.

Evaluate the following vignette and judge each of the 20 directed edges
(A -> B) on whether the vignette conveys A influencing B.

VIGNETTE
He sits across from me with his knees drawn to his chest, watching the afternoon light move across the office rug. When I ask how he's been since our last session, his gaze drifts to the window. The wind picks up outside, rattling the glass. He doesn't answer right away. His breath shallows. His hands, resting on his thighs, curl inward until his knuckles whiten. I recognize the shift in his posture immediately. The rain from three years ago is back. To Marco, the typhoon did not just damage his coastal hometown; it rewired his nervous system. He was seventeen when the storm surge breached the seawall. He remembers the sound first-a low, metallic groan that vibrated through his ribs-then the cold water seeping through his bedroom floor, the smell of wet drywall and rotting wood, his mother's voice cutting through the roar as the roof tore free above them. The memory does not visit him anymore. It occupies him. When a weather app on his phone pings a wind advisory, his heart launches against his sternum. He has deleted every weather application, uninstalled news sites, and changed his phone ringtones to pure silence. During the day, he drowns out the world with white noise and over-caffeinated routines. At night, he checks the deadbolt on his apartment door four times, then lies awake listening to the hum of the refrigerator, terrified of what silence might mean. He is twenty-two now, single, and navigating graduate-level coursework online. He tells his professors he attends lectures "sporadically due to health," which is technically true but only half the story. When the sky turns the color of bruised slate, he logs off, pulls the blackout curtains closed, and arranges his physical space with surgical precision. Chairs face the door. Windows are locked. A go-bag sits by the entryway, rotated monthly with canned goods, flashlights, and charged power banks. His family in the old neighborhood texts him updates about the rebuilt levees. In their messages, he hears the particular cadence of his mother's dialect, the way she always ends sentences with a soft sigh, as if speaking too loudly might summon the sky again. He reads them, then closes the thread. He cannot translate their relief into his own chest. At work, Marco is a UX designer for a regional transit application. His job requires him to map user journeys, anticipate friction, and build interfaces that feel seamless. He spends his days color-coding alert systems, writing microcopy that calms panic, and designing flows for emergency route updates. Clients praise his ability to make digital spaces feel safe. They do not know that every wireframe is an exercise in control. He arranges his own environment with the same intention: predictable, contained, exit-strategized. When a recent user test included a simulated network outage, Marco's fingers froze over the keyboard. The screen went dark, and for a breathless minute, he was back under the kitchen table, holding his younger sister's hands while the house groaned around them. He exhaled, rebooted his laptop, and logged out for the afternoon, telling his supervisor he needed a personal day. He tells himself it's a migraine. At twenty-two, he carries the weight of a collapsed coastline in his shoulders. He drinks his coffee black, skips social gatherings because he cannot stand the thought of being caught without an escape route, and sits on the floor of my office when his nervous system floods. He tells me that he just wants the quiet in his head to stop. The siren outside has faded. The rain has stopped. Marco's fingers tighten around his own wrists, then slowly uncurl. He does not look up when I ask if he heard the siren. He just nods, slow and heavy, and waits for the ground to feel steady again.

output.rationale: Triggering stimuli (e.g., weather alerts, sky color, network outage) directly evoke intrusive memories, threat responses, and maladaptive coping; negative appraisals (e.g., terror of silence) drive threat and avoidance; traumatic memories cause threat and avoidance; threat itself motivates maladaptive strategies.
